extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook treatment of schemes: what data a scheme consists of, how to view differentiable manifolds in the same language, the construction of Spec A as a set of prime ideals, basic examples (A^n, Spec Z), and foundational facts about localization, quotients, maps, and nilpotents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a scheme (three data items)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Thus we will define a scheme to be the following data: The set: the points of the scheme; The topology: the open sets of the scheme; The structure sheaf: the sheaf of “algebraic functions” (a sheaf of rings) on the scheme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall that a topological space with a sheaf of rings is called a ringed space (2.2.13). The structure sheaf is intended to encode the algebraic functions; later one must give the appropriate topology and sheaf axioms to complete the notion of scheme (affine patches, gluing, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiable manifold as a locally ringed space (definitional requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A differentiable real manifold may be defined as a topological space X with a sheaf of rings O_X (the sheaf of differentiable functions), together with a cover of X by open sets such that on each open set the ringed space is isomorphic to a ball around the origin in R^n (with the sheaf of differentiable functions on that ball).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the manifold-as-ringed-space viewpoint: the ball is the basic patch and a manifold is obtained by gluing these patches. In the usual manifold definition one also requires the underlying topological space to be Hausdorff; in the algebro-geometric analogue one often requires 'separatedness' to avoid analogous pathologies (see Chapter 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms of manifolds characterized by pullback of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous map π:X→Y between differentiable manifolds is a differentiable morphism if pullback of functions along π sends differentiable functions on Y to differentiable functions on X, i.e., pullback gives a map O_Y → O_X (equivalently π^{-1}O_Y → O_X or π^♯: O_Y → π_*O_X depending on viewpoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The important exercise 3.1.A states: show π is differentiable if differentiable functions pull back to differentiable functions. Exercise 3.1.B observes that the induced map on stalks sends the maximal ideal of O_{Y,q} into the maximal ideal of O_{X,p} when π(p)=q, reflecting the locally ringed nature of manifold morphisms. This gives a practical local test for differentiability of a continuous map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec A as underlying set: prime ideals as points and evaluation via residue classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec A is defined as the set of prime ideals of A (denoted [p] for a prime p). Elements a∈A are viewed as 'functions' on Spec A, and the value of a at the point [p] is a mod p (i.e., the image of a in A/p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint makes precise statements like: a function can take values in different rings at different points (e.g., 5 on Spec Z takes value 1 mod 2 at [(2)] and 2 mod 3 at [(3)]). One should be comfortable translating between 'a∈p' and 'a vanishes at [p]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinates and generators give geometric interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is generated over a base ring or field by elements x_1,...,x_r, these generators are often called coordinates because Spec A can be interpreted (via generators and relations) as a subset of affine space A^r (traditional points solving the relations) together with 'bonus' nontraditional points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates thinking of k[x_1,...,x_n]/(relations) as the coordinate ring of a variety embedded in A^n_k; pictures of traditional points are helpful heuristics though schemes also include extra points (generic points, nonclosed points). See Exercises and later sections for formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic point and maximal/closed points (interpretation of prime ideals)
rubrics_metrics.description: In integral domains like C[x], (0) is a prime ideal that serves as the 'generic point' (denoted [(0)]), while ideals of the form (x−a) are maximal ideals corresponding to the usual (closed) points. Smaller ideals correspond to bigger geometric points; containment of ideals reverses geometric inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The generic point is 'somewhere on the line but nowhere in particular' and is 'near' every point. Maximal ideals correspond to the traditional points (n-tuples of coordinates). Visual heuristics: for A^1_C, there is a traditional point for each a∈C plus the generic point; in higher dimensions prime ideals of various heights represent subvarieties of different dimensions (e.g., (0) highest-dimensional, principal primes codimension 1, maximal ideals dimension 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's Weak Nullstellensatz and Nullstellensatz (maximal ideals description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak Nullstellensatz (3.2.4): If k is algebraically closed, maximal ideals of k[x_1,...,x_n] are precisely of the form (x_1−a_1,...,x_n−a_n) for a_i∈k. Nullstellensatz (3.2.5): For any field k, every maximal ideal of k[x_1,...,x_n] has residue field a finite extension of k (equivalently, any finitely generated k-algebra that is a field is finite over k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results justify the intuition that closed points in affine n-space over an algebraically closed field correspond exactly to k-points. Use these theorems when identifying maximal ideals and when relating algebraic and geometric pictures; exercises show how the stronger Nullstellensatz implies the weak version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient rings and spectra: Spec(A/I) corresponds to subset of Spec(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prime ideals of A/I are in bijection with prime ideals of A containing I; thus Spec(A/I) can be pictured as the subset of Spec A consisting of primes containing I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: cutting out a closed subscheme corresponds to passing to a quotient ring. Exercise 3.2.J is 'essential' for understanding this correspondence and the inclusion-preserving nature of the bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization and distinguished opens: Spec(S^{-1}A) corresponds to primes disjoint from S
rubrics_metrics.description: Prime ideals of S^{-1}A are in bijection with prime ideals of A that do not meet the multiplicative set S. In particular, for S={1,f,f^2,...} the primes of A_f are those not containing f — i.e., the open locus where f does not vanish (a distinguished open). For S=A−p (localization at a prime p), primes of A_p correspond to primes of A contained in p (a 'germ' near p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use localization to picture removing loci (Af) or focusing near a point (A_p). Examples: Spec C[x,y]_{y−x^2} is the affine plane minus the parabola y−x^2; Spec C[x,y]_{(x,y)} is a 'shred' near the origin preserving curves through the origin. Exercises 3.2.K and 3.2.L develop these correspondences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality: maps of rings induce maps of spectra in the opposite direction
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring homomorphism φ:B→A induces a map of sets Spec A → Spec B by sending a prime p⊂A to its preimage φ^{-1}(p), giving a contravariant functor from rings to sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the seed of the notion of morphisms of schemes: formulas/coordinate maps correspond to ring maps and hence to maps of spectra. Examples and exercises (3.2.O, 3.2.P) illustrate explicit coordinate ring maps and the induced maps on points (evaluation via substituted polynomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps between affine varieties correspond to polynomial coordinate maps (explicit description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a k-algebra homomorphism φ:k[y_1,...,y_n]→k[x_1,...,x_m] defined by y_i ↦ f_i(x_1,...,x_m), φ induces a map Spec k[x_1,...,x_m]/I → Spec k[y_1,...,y_n]/J provided φ(J)⊂I; on traditional (closed) points it sends (a_1,...,a_m) to (f_1(a),...,f_n(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concrete way to construct geometric maps from algebraic formulas. Example 3.2.10 and the exercises show how classical maps (e.g., projection, x↦x^2) translate to ring maps and how fibers over points can be analyzed via these maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec Z as a family (bundle) of affine spaces over Spec Z; fibers over primes
rubrics_metrics.description: The map π: A^n_Z = Spec Z[x_1,...,x_n] → Spec Z exhibits A^n_Z as a 'family' of A^n's; the fiber π^{-1}([(p)]) is canonically identified with A^n_{F_p} and the fiber over (0) corresponds to the geometric generic fiber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint helps visualize schemes over Spec Z as families parameterized by primes; Exercise 3.2.Q makes this precise. It is useful for thinking about reduction modulo p and how geometric properties vary in families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions not determined pointwise: nilpotents and the nilradical
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring element that vanishes at every prime (i.e., at every point of Spec A) need not be zero: precisely those elements are nilpotent. The nilradical N(A) equals the intersection of all prime ideals of A (Theorem 3.2.12). Two functions have the same values at points iff they differ by a nilpotent. A ring with no nonzero nilpotents is called reduced, and then functions are determined by their values at points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: k[ε]/(ε^2) has ε≠0 but ε vanishes at all points. Exercises 3.2.R and 3.2.S justify that nilpotents do not change the underlying set (Spec B ≅ Spec B/N) and characterize the failure of pointwise-determination precisely. This is crucial to adjust naive geometric intuition when working with schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension heuristics via prime ideals and containment (geometric interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prime ideals of different heights correspond to geometric loci of different dimensions (e.g., in C[x,y,z] maximal ideals are 0-dimensional points, principal irreducible ideals give hypersurfaces of codimension 1, (0) corresponds to the full n-dimensional space). Containment of prime ideals corresponds to inclusion of the associated geometric loci but with reverse order: larger ideals give smaller loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a precise definition of dimension is given later (Chapter 11), the text repeatedly urges the reader to visualize primes of various sizes as points, curves, hypersurfaces, etc. Exercises show concrete examples (e.g., (x,y) as the z-axis in C[x,y,z]). Keep in mind the order-reversal phenomenon: ideal containment reverses geometric containment.
